titleStmt.title: Memorandum From the President’s Assistant for National Security Affairs (Poindexter) to President Reagan

div.head: 454. Memorandum From the President’s Assistant for National Security Affairs (Poindexter) to President Reagan
div.p: Meeting with Uruguayan President Julio Maria Sanguinetti
To support Uruguay’s return to democracy, to strengthen bilateral relations, to bring Uruguay more firmly into the West, to explain our policies on Central America and terrorism.

President Julio Sanguinetti, Uruguay’s first civilian President in 12 years, is a serious, articulate statesman who is pragmatic, moderate and generally friendly to the West and the United States. Uruguay’s almost century-long democratic tradition was interrupted when the military seized power in 1973 following several years of economic decline, labor agitation and urban guerrilla (Tupamaros) violence. Uruguay’s political leaders have traditionally espoused a social democratic philosophy which led to an extensive social welfare system that eventually became unsustainable and an economy dominated by the state which grew in inefficiency over the decades. One only has to drive through the lovely capital city, Montevideo, to see how tarnished Uruguay’s reputation as the “Switzerland of Latin America” has become: once handsome homes and buildings now shabby and crumbling, boarded-up small stores and factories, youth idle in the streets. President Sanguinetti’s bold and skillful leadership has bolstered his political position but large challenges remain. You invited him for a state visit in a letter delivered to him by Secretary Shultz at Sanguinetti’s inauguration in March 1985 as a concrete gesture of support for Uruguay’s return to democracy, a theme which we anticipate will dominate this state visit.

Return to Democracy and Consolidation: President Sanguinetti and his Colorado Party played an active role in the transition to democracy by helping negotiate a face-saving formula for the military to relinquish power by allowing it limited participation in the government. The Uruguayan electorate remains pluralist; there are three
major parties, the traditional Colorado and Blanco parties, and the newer Broad Front, a coalition of leftist groups spanning the ideological spectrum from democratic socialism to Marxism-Leninism. A “National Accord” between the three parties signed last April has been badly eroded over the past two months, making Sanguinetti’s ability to maintain opposition support in the Congress difficult. Although rebuilding the economy is his principal long-term challenge, labor unrest is the greatest immediate problem. Aggressive leftwing union leaders and communists called over 200 strikes and organized 223 new unions in the first six months of the Sanguinetti administration. Labor leaders are planning a general strike on June 17, the day of your meeting with Sanguinetti. Sanguinetti has also had to walk a fine line between meeting demands from the left and appeasing an apprehensive military, which is concerned about leftist demands for Argentine-style trials of officers for alleged human rights abuses committed under the military regime. Long-term prospects for stability in Uruguay are uncertain at best. During your meeting with Sanguinetti, you could show sympathy for the challenges he faces in consolidating democratic rule in Uruguay.

The Economy and US Assistance: During his first year in office, President Sanguinetti implemented modest free market reforms and austerity measures that enabled Uruguay to obtain an IMF-supported stabilization program and arrange for new commercial loans. Cheaper oil imports and lower interest rates will probably generate economic growth this year of roughly two percent while the government’s anti-inflationary wage policies will hold down price increases. Despite these accomplishments, Montevideo has not implemented the basic reforms needed to make the Uruguayan economy internationally competitive: pruning back the public sector and overblown welfare programs, giving concrete production incentives to private entrepreneurs, and diversifying exports. Domestic and congressional opposition will make it difficult for him to address these problems.

The Uruguayan government has publicly stated its desire for foreign investment and since 1985, we have been negotiating with them on what would be the first Bilateral Investment Treaty (BIT) in South America. The BIT will in all likelihood not be ready for signing during President Sanguinetti’s visit and has become a sensitive issue in Uruguay. The Foreign Minister has requested that we not publicly mention the BIT but you could privately encourage a BIT as an important step in attracting US investors to Uruguay.

Trade issues are the primary irritant in relations. Uruguay appreciates that we are its largest customer, but is deeply concerned about protectionism and falling prices for its products. They are especially concerned about the negative impact of the export provisions of the Farm Act, particularly the Export Enhancement Program (EEP) and the rice and dairy programs. You can tell President Sanguinetti that there were sections of the Farm Bill which you did not support, and that the Executive Branch has formulated its programs to minimize the harm caused to non-subsidizing exporters. You can tell him as well that we believe the new trade round is the best hope to iron out problems in agricultural trade and that we are pleased that Uruguay will host the GATT Ministerial in September. You might mention that we expect to join together in our concern about EC agricultural policies, and that we would appreciate their support on services.

The US will provide Uruguay $14.4 million in Economic Support Funds (ESF) and this agreement will be signed during the state visit. We have a small MAP (military assistance) program that will assist President Sanguinetti to demonstrate to the military that democracy yields some rewards. President Sanguinetti is not aware that we have arranged for you to show our support for Uruguay with some small gestures that you may choose to mention during the meeting:

list.item: a program which Sanguinetti just requested to provide top business and academic agricultural experts to consult on modernization is available,
a longstanding countervailing duty issue regarding leather wearing apparel can be lifted,
the temporary cheese quota granted to Uruguay in 1985 has been slightly increased and is a permanent quota,
Trade Development Program funds for feasibility studies related to development projects are available as well.

div.p: Foreign Policy and Central America: Besides maintaining Uruguay’s traditionally close relations with the United States and Western Europe, Sanguinetti is paying greater attention to regional issues. Its position of leadership in the Cartagena Group on the debt issue has permitted it to exert a moderating influence. It has played a minor role in the Contadora Support Group. Uruguay has also strengthened relations with the Soviet bloc and established relations with Cuba after a 21-year hiatus in order to placate Uruguay’s domestic leftists.

Sanguinetti and his government appear to be particularly fearful of a US invasion of Nicaragua because of the impact they believe this would have on domestic Uruguayan politics. They oppose US assistance to the contras. You can reassure him that the United States has no intention to intervene militarily in Central America. You can point out that South Americans talk to you about democracy, but seem to draw the line when it comes to supporting a democratic outcome in Nicaragua. You might suggest to Sanguinetti that if he cannot openly support the resistance, you hope he might refrain from publicly opposing our efforts to assist them.

The Soviets, Terrorism and Libya: We want the new Latin American democracies to feel that they are part of the “inner circle” of Western democracies by discussing high priority issues with them. You can explain to Sanguinetti that improving our relationship with the Soviets is a long-term task and that we are prepared to be patient. Sanguinetti will most likely welcome being better informed about your decision on Interim Restraint based on Soviet noncompliance on arms control treaties. You can assure him that the US will continue to exercise utmost restraint while protecting strategic deterrence and working for reductions in strategic arsenals on both sides.

Sanguinetti publicly criticized our military actions against Libya. You might explain to him that we are making concentrated efforts with our allies to combat state-supported terrorism and because we share Uruguay’s belief that international cooperation is necessary to successfully combat terrorism. Irrefutable evidence indicates Sandinista support to Colombia’s M–19 in Palace of Justice incident.

Short One-on-One: Your Ambassador in Uruguay, Judge Malcolm Wilkey, suggested that a short one-on-one with Sanguinetti about Central America, after the Oval Office meeting concludes and the participants are walking to the departure area, will help him understand the significance of this matter to the US government and underscore our determination to see democracy flourish in Nicaragua. You might emphasize to him once again your belief that US military intervention in Central America will not be necessary if the democracies of this hemisphere work together to produce a democracy in Nicaragua. You could explain that our national security concerns about Nicaragua extend to concerns about the security of South America’s new democracies because of Sandinista expansionist tendencies.
[Omitted here are a list of participants, a press plan, and a sequence of events.]

note.p: Source: Reagan Library, NSC Records, Latin American Affairs Directorate, Presidential File, Presidential Appointments: Meeting with Uruguayan President Sanguinetti 06/1986. Secret. Prepared by Tillman. Copies were sent to Bush and Regan. Reagan wrote his initials at the top of the first page. A stamped notation at the top of the memorandum indicates that Reagan saw it on June 17. Attached as Tab B, but not printed are talking points. Attached as Tab C, but not printed, are biographies. Tillman sent the memorandum to Poindexter for signature under cover of a June 13 memorandum.

In telegram 3137 from Montevideo, May 23, the Embassy reported on Whitehead’s May 22–23 meetings with Sanguinetti, Iglesias, and Zerbino, writing: “The Sanguinetti government has accomplished a great deal in its first year in power. Uruguayan democracy is healthy, thanks in large part to the cooperation of the opposition political parties and the military. Although the economy is still sluggish, Sanguinetti has reversed decades of statist stultification and set Uruguay on a sensible path toward economic growth.” Whitehead noted “the fact is that Uruguayan exports to the US have increased by 70 percent since 1982; we are now Uruguay’s leading export market; and we import twice as much from Uruguay as we export to them. How, I asked the Foreign Minister, can we then be accused of protectionism? Iglesias responded that he fully realized that the US economy was far more open than the EC or Japan, and promised that both he and Sanguinetti would make this clear during next month’s visit.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, N860005–0564)
